---
title: "Case Study: The Ravens' Option Run Game with Lamar Jackson (2019–2025)"
subtitle: "How Baltimore turned a quarterback's legs into an extra blocker on every snap, what it won, what defenses did about it, and how the era ended"
description: "A closed-era case study of the 2019–2025 Baltimore Ravens: the problem of fitting Lamar Jackson into a conventional offense, Greg Roman's 2019 rebuild (heavy personnel, the pistol, a menu of option reads and designed quarterback runs), why a running quarterback changes the arithmetic of every run fit, the signature plays (pistol inverted veer, 13-personnel sets, QB counter), the data fingerprint from nflverse (rushing EPA against the league every season from 2018 to 2025), the defensive answers (speed, deficits, pressure and spies), Todd Monken's 2023 changes and the Derrick Henry seasons, an honest look at the playoffs, and what survives into 2026."
glossary:
  "Pistol option offense": "An offense that makes the pistol its base alignment and builds its run game on the quarterback as a runner: option reads (zone read, bash, power read, counter read) and designed quarterback runs, usually with tight ends and fullbacks as extra blockers, so that the defense must account for one more ball carrier on every snap. The 2019–2022 Baltimore Ravens under Greg Roman are the NFL's defining example; Chris Ault's Nevada teams built the college version."

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
#| output: false
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style

OL_NAMES = {"LT": "LT", "LG": "LG", "C": "C", "RG": "RG", "RT": "RT"}
GREEN = "#0f7a55"           # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]    # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange


def named_line(players):
    """Label the five offensive linemen so the reader can follow each one."""
    return [p.moved(label=OL_NAMES[p.key]) if p.key in OL_NAMES else p for p in players]


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    return [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in OL_NAMES]


def pistol(extra=(), te=("Y", "U")):
    """The pistol box: five linemen, the quarterback 4 yards deep, the back 7 yards deep directly behind him,
    and inline tight ends (Y on the right, U on the left). Receivers are left out unless passed in `extra`."""
    tes = []
    if "Y" in te:
        tes.append(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"))
    if "U" in te:
        tes.append(O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"))
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -4.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), *tes, *extra]


def front62(fs=False):
    """Eight in the box against two tight ends: a 9-technique outside each tight end, a 5 on each tackle,
    a 1 and a 3 inside, and two linebackers (a 6-2 look). Optional free safety in the deep middle."""
    dfn = [D("BE", "OLB", 1.0, -6.3, "9"), D("B5", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "5"), D("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"),
           D("DT3", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"), D("P5", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "5"), D("PE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.3, "9"),
           D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W")]
    if fs:
        dfn.append(D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS"))
    return dfn


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven offensive players on the line, and only the two at its ends may be eligible receivers."""
    off = [q for q in players if q.side == "off"]
    on = sorted([q for q in off if q.d > -1.0], key=lambda q: q.w)
    assert len(on) == 7, [q.key for q in on]
    for q in on[1:-1]:
        assert q.key in OL_NAMES, f"{q.key} is covered up but not a lineman"


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path, run or pull."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run, "pull": p.pull}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, label=None, label_at=None, lw=2.0, fontsize=7.5,
           dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), zorder=6):
    """A dashed 'option' path through absolute (d, w) points, with an arrowhead."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=zorder, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=11, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=zorder))
    if label:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, *(label_at or pts[-1]))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, label, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, fontweight="bold", ha="center",
                    va="center", zorder=9,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=0.8))


def read_line(fld, p, a, b, color=style.THIRD):
    """The quarterback's eyes: a dashed green line between two (d, w) spots."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=4)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7, weight="normal"):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def tackle_x(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK):
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=10, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)


def box_shade(fld, p, d0, d1, w0, w1, color=GREEN):
    """Shade the box (alignment coordinates) to count defenders against blockers."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=0.07,
                               ec=color, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips and videos (as in 03-04)
MARK_R = 0.6   # frame-strip marker radius in yards


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def carrier(play, t):
    """Who holds the ball at time t (QB until the first handoff or pitch arrives)."""
    holder = "QB"
    for kind, to, te in sorted(play.ball_events, key=lambda e: e[2]):
        if t >= te + (0.25 if kind == "pitch" else 0.0):
            holder = to
    return holder


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails, the ball, rings (and a green ring on the ball carrier)."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.4, play.los + window[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")
                & df["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1])]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.5), 0.75, 0.45, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in list(rings) + [(carrier(play, t), style.THIRD)]:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key]
        if len(rr):
            x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"].iloc[0], rr["y"].iloc[0])
            ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), width_in=6.5, ncols=2):
    """Frame strip of one simulated play, wrapped over rows, with a caption line under each panel."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.6 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for k, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        ax.set_title(f"{k + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[k], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.2,
                    color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.5)
    return fig


def video(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), width_in=5.4):
    """Web version: the same panel drawn every tenth of a second, with the current step's note."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    grid = np.round(np.arange(float(df["time"].min()), float(df["time"].max()) + 1e-9, 0.1), 2)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.6))

    def update(t):
        ax.clear()
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [m for tt, m in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=list(grid), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_animation(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, lateral, window, notes=notes, rings=rings, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, lateral, window, notes=notes, rings=rings)
```

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the chapter's data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2018, 2026))
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "week", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "defteam", "play_type", "epa", "success",
        "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "aborted_play", "down", "ydstogo", "rusher_player_id", "rusher_player_name",
        "passer_player_name", "rush", "pass", "yards_gained", "rushing_yards", "run_location", "wp",
        "half_seconds_remaining", "qtr", "score_differential", "fumble_lost", "interception"]
ALL = pbp(SEASONS, columns=COLS)
ALL = ALL[ALL["play_type"].isin(["run", "pass"]) & ALL["down"].notna() & ALL["epa"].notna() & (ALL["qb_kneel"] == 0)]
ALL["designed"] = (ALL["rush"] == 1) & (ALL["qb_scramble"] == 0) & (ALL["aborted_play"] == 0)
REG = ALL[ALL["season_type"] == "REG"]
POST = ALL[ALL["season_type"] == "POST"]
RUNS = REG[REG["designed"]]

# --- rushing EPA per designed run, every team, every season
TEAM_RUN = RUNS.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean().rename("epa").reset_index()
TEAM_RUN["rank"] = TEAM_RUN.groupby("season")["epa"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
LG_RUN = RUNS.groupby("season")["epa"].mean()
BAL_RUN = TEAM_RUN[TEAM_RUN["posteam"] == "BAL"].set_index("season")
BAL_SR = RUNS[RUNS["posteam"] == "BAL"].groupby("season")["success"].mean()
LG_SR = RUNS.groupby("season")["success"].mean()
ALL_EPA_RANK = (REG.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean().groupby("season").rank(ascending=False)
                .xs("BAL", level=1).astype(int))
RUSH_YDS_RANK = (REG.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["rushing_yards"].sum().groupby("season")
                 .rank(ascending=False, method="min").xs("BAL", level=1).astype(int))

# 2018: Joe Flacco started weeks 1-10, Lamar Jackson weeks 11-17
B18 = REG[(REG["season"] == 2018) & (REG["posteam"] == "BAL")]
R18 = {lab: (B18[m]["designed"].mean(), B18[m & B18["designed"]]["epa"].mean())
       for lab, m in [("flacco", B18["week"] <= 10), ("jackson", B18["week"] >= 11)]}

# designed runs by everyone but the quarterbacks (anyone with 20+ dropbacks for that team that season)
_qbs = set(REG[REG["passer_player_name"].notna()].groupby(["season", "posteam", "passer_player_name"]).size()
           .loc[lambda x: x >= 20].reset_index()["passer_player_name"])
_nq = RUNS[~RUNS["rusher_player_name"].isin(_qbs)]
_nqt = _nq.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean()
NQ_BAL = _nqt.xs("BAL", level=1)
NQ_RANK = _nqt.groupby("season").rank(ascending=False).xs("BAL", level=1).astype(int)
NQ_LG = _nq.groupby("season")["epa"].mean()

# neutral early downs: run share
NEU = REG[REG["down"].isin([1, 2]) & REG["wp"].between(0.2, 0.8) & (REG["half_seconds_remaining"] > 120)]
NEU_RR = NEU.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["designed"].mean()
NEU_RANK = NEU_RR.groupby("season").rank(ascending=False, method="min").xs("BAL", level=1).astype(int)
NEU_BAL = NEU_RR.xs("BAL", level=1)
NEU_LG = NEU.groupby("season")["designed"].mean()

# dropbacks (everything that isn't a designed run: passes, sacks, scrambles)
_DB = REG[~REG["designed"]].groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean()
DB_BAL = _DB.xs("BAL", level=1)
DB_RANK = _DB.groupby("season").rank(ascending=False).xs("BAL", level=1).astype(int)
DB_LG = REG[~REG["designed"]].groupby("season")["epa"].mean()

# --- Lamar Jackson's designed runs (no scrambles, botched snaps or likely sneaks), per game he played
BAL = ALL[ALL["posteam"] == "BAL"]
LJ = BAL[(BAL["rusher_player_name"] == "L.Jackson") & BAL["designed"]
         & ~((BAL["ydstogo"] <= 2) & (BAL["run_location"] == "middle"))]
LJ_REG = LJ[LJ["season_type"] == "REG"]
LJ_GAMES = BAL[(BAL["season_type"] == "REG") & (BAL["passer_player_name"] == "L.Jackson")].groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique()
LJ_N = LJ_REG.groupby("season").size()
LJ_PG = (LJ_N / LJ_GAMES)
LJ_EPA = LJ_REG.groupby("season")["epa"].mean()
LJ_YPC = LJ_REG.groupby("season")["yards_gained"].mean()

# --- participation (personnel, formation, box count); NGS through 2022, FTN from 2023
parts = []
for yr in SEASONS:
    pa = nfl().load_participation([yr]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel",
                                                     "defense_personnel", "offense_formation", "defenders_in_box"]]
    parts.append(pa)
PART = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True).rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
RP = REG.merge(PART, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
_s = RP["offense_personnel"].fillna("")
RP["wr"] = _s.str.extract(r"(\d+) WR")[0].astype(float)
RP.loc[_s == "", "wr"] = np.nan
RP["heavy"] = (RP["wr"] < 3).where(RP["wr"].notna())
HEAVY = RP.groupby(["season", RP["posteam"] == "BAL"])["heavy"].mean().unstack()   # columns False (others), True (BAL)
LG_HEAVY = RP.groupby("season")["heavy"].mean()
PISTOL_NGS = RP[RP["season"] <= 2022].assign(p=lambda x: x["offense_formation"] == "PISTOL")
PISTOL_BAL = PISTOL_NGS[PISTOL_NGS["posteam"] == "BAL"].groupby("season")["p"].mean()
PISTOL_LG = PISTOL_NGS.groupby("season")["p"].mean()
P19 = PISTOL_NGS[(PISTOL_NGS["season"] == 2019) & PISTOL_NGS["p"]].groupby("posteam").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
B19 = RP[(RP["season"] == 2019) & (RP["posteam"] == "BAL")]
L19 = RP[RP["season"] == 2019]
PIST19_RUN = (B19[B19["designed"]]["offense_formation"] == "PISTOL").mean()
P13 = B19[B19["offense_personnel"] == "1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR"]
P13_PASS = 1 - P13["designed"].mean()
L13_PASS = 1 - L19[L19["offense_personnel"] == "1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR"]["designed"].mean()
P13_BASE = P13["defense_personnel"].fillna("").str.contains("4 DB").mean()
BASE_BAL19 = B19["defense_personnel"].fillna("").str.contains(r"\b4 DB").mean()
BASE_LG19 = L19["defense_personnel"].fillna("").str.contains(r"\b4 DB").mean()
_NGS = RP[(RP["season"] <= 2022) & RP["defense_personnel"].notna()]
_NGS = _NGS.assign(base=_NGS["defense_personnel"].str.contains(r"\b4 DB"))
BASE_BY = _NGS.groupby(["season", _NGS["posteam"] == "BAL"])["base"].mean().unstack()   # NGS labels, 2018-2022
P11_RUN_BAL = B19[B19["offense_personnel"] == "1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR"]["designed"].mean()
P11_RUN_LG = L19[L19["offense_personnel"] == "1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR"]["designed"].mean()
BOX = RP[RP["designed"] & (RP["defenders_in_box"] >= 3)]
BOX_BAL = BOX[BOX["posteam"] == "BAL"].groupby("season")["defenders_in_box"].mean()
BOX_LG = BOX.groupby("season")["defenders_in_box"].mean()
BOX8_BAL = (BOX[BOX["posteam"] == "BAL"]["defenders_in_box"] >= 8).groupby(BOX[BOX["posteam"] == "BAL"]["season"]).mean()
BOX8_LG = (BOX["defenders_in_box"] >= 8).groupby(BOX["season"]).mean()

# --- FTN charting 2022-2025: where the quarterback stood (U = under center, S = shotgun, P = pistol)
FTN = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
FTN = FTN.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"}).drop(columns=["season", "week"])
RF = REG[REG["season"] >= 2022].merge(FTN[["game_id", "play_id", "qb_location", "n_offense_backfield"]],
                                      on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
QBLOC = RF.groupby(["season", RF["posteam"] == "BAL"])["qb_location"].value_counts(normalize=True).unstack().fillna(0)
HENRY = RF[(RF["posteam"] == "BAL") & (RF["rusher_player_name"] == "D.Henry") & RF["designed"]]
HENRY_LOC = HENRY.groupby("qb_location").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), ypc=("yards_gained", "mean"))
BAL_RUN_UC = RF[(RF["posteam"] == "BAL") & RF["designed"]].groupby("season")["qb_location"].apply(lambda s: (s == "U").mean())

# --- playoffs
GAMES = nfl().load_schedules(SEASONS).to_pandas()
GB = GAMES[(GAMES["home_team"] == "BAL") | (GAMES["away_team"] == "BAL")].copy()
GB["bal"] = np.where(GB["home_team"] == "BAL", GB["home_score"], GB["away_score"])
GB["opp_pts"] = np.where(GB["home_team"] == "BAL", GB["away_score"], GB["home_score"])
GB["opp"] = np.where(GB["home_team"] == "BAL", GB["away_team"], GB["home_team"])
REC = GB[GB["game_type"] == "REG"].groupby("season").apply(lambda g: (int((g.bal > g.opp_pts).sum()), int((g.bal < g.opp_pts).sum())))
PO = GB[GB["game_type"] != "REG"].set_index("game_id")
BP = POST[POST["posteam"] == "BAL"]
REG_LJ = REG[(REG["posteam"] == "BAL") & ~((REG["season"] == 2018) & (REG["week"] < 11))]


def game_line(x):
    return pd.Series({"epa": x["epa"].mean(), "run_epa": x[x["designed"]]["epa"].mean(),
                      "run_rate": x["designed"].mean(), "to": x["fumble_lost"].sum() + x["interception"].sum(),
                      "trail8": (x["score_differential"] < -7).mean(), "plays": len(x)})


PO_LINES = BP.groupby("game_id").apply(game_line).join(PO[["season", "game_type", "gameday", "opp", "bal", "opp_pts"]])
PO_LINES = PO_LINES.sort_values("gameday")
REG_LINE = game_line(REG_LJ)
REG_GAMES = REG_LJ["game_id"].nunique()
POST_LINE = game_line(BP)
LJ_PO = PO_LINES[PO_LINES.index != "2022_19_BAL_CIN"]
LJ_PO_W = int((LJ_PO["bal"] > LJ_PO["opp_pts"]).sum())
LJ_PO_L = int((LJ_PO["bal"] < LJ_PO["opp_pts"]).sum())
LOSSES = PO_LINES[PO_LINES["bal"] < PO_LINES["opp_pts"]]
# Drill 3: designed runs against light boxes (six or fewer), and runs v dropbacks when trailing by 8+
_light = RP[RP["designed"] & RP["defenders_in_box"].between(3, 6) & (RP["season"] >= 2019)]
LIGHT_BAL = _light[_light["posteam"] == "BAL"]["epa"].mean()
LIGHT_LG = _light["epa"].mean()
_tr = REG_LJ[REG_LJ["score_differential"] < -7]
TR_RUN, TR_DB = _tr[_tr["designed"]]["epa"].mean(), _tr[~_tr["designed"]]["epa"].mean()
TO3_LOSSES = int((LOSSES["to"] >= 3).sum())
# run share by score: within one score (a touchdown either way) and when not trailing
CLOSE_REG = REG_LJ[REG_LJ["score_differential"].between(-7, 7)]["designed"].mean()
CLOSE_POST = BP[BP["score_differential"].between(-7, 7)]["designed"].mean()
# playoff designed runs without the two games in which the run was stuffed (Jan 2019 LAC, Jan 2020 TEN)
_bp2 = BP[~BP["game_id"].isin(["2018_18_LAC_BAL", "2019_19_TEN_BAL"])]
PO_RUN_EX2 = _bp2[_bp2["designed"]]["epa"].mean()
# the league baseline: how much worse does a typical playoff offense play in January? (2018-2024 seasons)
_post = POST[POST["season"] <= 2024].groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean()
_reg = REG[REG["season"] <= 2024].groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].mean()
LG_PO_DROP = (_post - _reg.reindex(_post.index)).mean()
# Baltimore's own regular season against teams that made the playoffs that year
_po_teams = {(s_, t) for s_, g in GAMES[GAMES["game_type"] != "REG"].groupby("season")
             for t in set(g["home_team"]) | set(g["away_team"])}
REG_VS_PO = REG_LJ[[(s_, t) in _po_teams for s_, t in zip(REG_LJ["season"], REG_LJ["defteam"])]]["epa"].mean()

# the December 1, 2019 film room (49ers at Ravens)
_sf = RP[(RP["game_id"] == "2019_13_SF_BAL") & (RP["posteam"] == "BAL")]
SF19 = {"pistol": (_sf["offense_formation"] == "PISTOL").mean(), "run_rate": _sf["designed"].mean()}


def one_game(gid):
    """Baltimore's designed-run EPA and Jackson's designed runs in one game."""
    g = ALL[(ALL["game_id"] == gid) & (ALL["posteam"] == "BAL")]
    lj = g[(g["rusher_player_name"] == "L.Jackson") & g["designed"]]
    return {"run_epa": g[g["designed"]]["epa"].mean(), "runs": int(g["designed"].sum()),
            "lj_n": len(lj), "lj_yds": int(lj["yards_gained"].sum()),
            "lj_all_n": int((g["rusher_player_name"] == "L.Jackson").sum()),
            "lj_all_yds": int(g[g["rusher_player_name"] == "L.Jackson"]["yards_gained"].sum())}


MIA21, KC24, DET25R = one_game("2021_10_BAL_MIA"), one_game("2024_01_BAL_KC"), one_game("2025_03_DET_BAL")


# --- formatting helpers for the inline numbers
def sg(x, n=2):
    return f"{x:+.{n}f}"


def pct(x):
    return f"{100 * x:.0f}%"


def ordinal(n):
    n = int(n)
    return f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"


def rec(season):
    w, l = REC.loc[season]
    return f"{w}–{l}"
```

Picture a typical Sunday in the fall of 2019. Baltimore breaks the huddle with two tight ends.
Lamar Jackson stands four yards behind the center, with Mark Ingram directly behind *him*, three yards deeper.
The defense has seen the film. It walks a safety down and crowds eight men within a few yards of the ball, the
kind of picture a broadcaster calls "selling out to stop the run." The ball is snapped, Jackson puts it in
Ingram's stomach, and an unblocked defensive end on the edge freezes for half a heartbeat, unsure whether to
take the back or the quarterback. Ingram goes for seven. Two plays later, from the same look, the same end
crashes on Ingram, and Jackson is past him and gone for twenty. The defense did what every coaching manual
says, loaded the box, and lost anyway. **How do you build an offense where "eight in the box" is not enough,
and why did it beat the NFL for five years and then, in the games that mattered most, too often come up
short?** This chapter is that story, told as a closed era: the 2019–2025 Ravens, from Greg Roman's rebuild to
John Harbaugh's firing in January 2026.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain the four pieces of Greg Roman's 2019 design (heavy personnel, the pistol, a menu of option reads,
  designed quarterback runs) and what problem each one solved.
- Count a Ravens run the way their opponents had to: blockers, plus the quarterback as a runner, against
  defenders in the box, and say where the defense's extra man has to come from.
- Recognize the signature plays (the pistol inverted veer, the 13-personnel sets, the QB counter) from the
  formation and the first step of the line.
- Read the era's data fingerprint (rushing EPA against the league every season, Jackson's designed runs, the
  pistol and under-center shares) and say what changed under Todd Monken in 2023 and with
  Derrick Henry in 2024.
- Describe the defenses' answers (speed, deficits, pressure, spies) and judge the "can't win in the playoffs"
  argument with the numbers rather than the narrative.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd)**: the read key, give and keep, the
  [zone read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-read), the
  [inverted veer](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-inverted-veer) (power read), and designed quarterback runs
  ([QB power](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-power), [QB counter](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-counter))
  as a way to turn the running back into a blocker. This case study assumes you can tell those apart.
- **[Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)**:
  every gap owned exactly once, the [**plus-one**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-plus-one) (one more run
  defender than the offense has blockers), and the rule "count the quarterback as a blocker when he reads."
- **[The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd)**: the league these Ravens played in, from the 2018
  passing boom to the two-high defenses and the return of heavy personnel and under-center snaps by 2025.

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; *left* and *right* mean the
offense's left and right. Q is the quarterback and R the running back; Y and U are tight ends (Y on the right,
U on the left) and H a third tight end on the wing. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the linemen. Defensive linemen are
labelled by their technique number (9 is the end man outside a tight end, 5 on a tackle's outside shoulder, 3
on a guard's, 1 shaded on the center); M and W are the Mike and Will linebackers, S the Sam, and FS and SS the
free and strong safeties. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks (a pulling lineman's path also ends in a bar,
where he makes his block), thin arrows are paths without the ball, thick dark arrows are ball carriers, and the
**dashed green line from the quarterback is his eyes**: the defender he is reading. Dashed arrows are an option's
*branches*. A **dotted brown line is the ball in the air** on a pass, and a **dotted orange line ties a defender to
the man he covers** in man coverage. Rings: **orange** marks the defender to watch, **purple** a blocker to
follow, and **green** follows the ball in the animation. Wide receivers who do not matter to the play are left out
of the box-sized pictures; they stand *off* the line of scrimmage, so the inline tight ends are the ends of the
line and eligible to catch a pass. Every picture is a typical version of a play, not a copy of a particular
Ravens snap.

## The problem: a quarterback who didn't fit (2018)

Lamar Jackson arrived in Baltimore with the last pick of the first round of the 2018 draft, 32nd overall, after
a Heisman Trophy at Louisville in 2016 and a college career in which he ran for more than 4,000 yards.[^draft]
He also arrived with a question hanging over him that a lot of NFL people asked out loud: could a quarterback
who ran like that be a real NFL passer, or would he have to move to another position? The loudest version came
from the Hall of Fame executive Bill Polian, who said that February that Jackson should switch to wide receiver
(and admitted in 2019 that he had been wrong).[^polian]
The Ravens had a veteran starter, Joe Flacco, a Super Bowl MVP five years earlier, and an offense built for a
pocket passer.

Then, in November 2018, Flacco hurt his hip, and on November 18 against Cincinnati Jackson made his first
NFL start.[^draft2] What followed was improvised. The coaching staff, with Marty Mornhinweg as offensive
coordinator, didn't have a Jackson offense, so it bolted
his college game onto Flacco's: lots of quarterback runs, read plays, extra tight ends, and as few
dropbacks as it could get away with. The data shows how sudden the swerve was. With Flacco starting, weeks 1
through 10, the Ravens called a designed run on `{python} pct(R18["flacco"][0])` of their plays; with Jackson
starting, weeks 11 through 17, it was `{python} pct(R18["jackson"][0])`. The runs also got better. Measured in
**EPA** per play ([expected points added](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa): how much a play raised or lowered
the number of points the offense could expect to score on the drive, the yardstick
[01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) introduced), they went from
`{python} sg(R18["flacco"][1])`, slightly worse than an average snap, to
`{python} sg(R18["jackson"][1])`.[^calc18] Jackson ran 147 times that season, a record for a
quarterback at the time, and Baltimore won six of his seven starts to take the AFC North.

The improvisation had a ceiling, and the wild-card game on January 6, 2019 found it. The Los Angeles Chargers had
played Baltimore two weeks earlier, and for the rematch their defensive coordinator, Gus Bradley, did something
almost nobody did: he put **seven defensive backs** on the field for 58 of the Ravens' 59 snaps, with two
safeties playing linebacker. The Chargers had used seven defensive backs for a total of 50 snaps all season.
Their head coach, Anthony Lynn, said later that when Bradley proposed it his first reaction was to ask whether
the staff was insane. It wasn't. The Ravens gained 90 rushing yards and 229 in total, the fewest the Chargers
had ever allowed in a playoff game, Jackson was sacked seven times, and Los Angeles won 23–17 after leading
23–3 in the fourth quarter.[^chargers] (@fig-seven-db, later in the chapter, draws the idea.)

The lesson the Ravens took from that afternoon was not "stop running the quarterback." It was that a run
game *added on* to an offense is a run game a defense can study, match and outnumber in a week. If Jackson's
legs were going to be the foundation, the whole offense had to be built on them, including the passing game,
so that the defense's best answer to the run would open something else. That is a design problem, and the man
the Ravens handed it to had been working on exactly that problem for most of a decade.

## The scheme answer: Greg Roman's 2019 rebuild

In January 2019 the Ravens promoted **Greg Roman**, their assistant head coach and tight ends coach, to
offensive coordinator in Mornhinweg's place.[^roman] Roman had run the 49ers' offense from 2011 to 2014, when Colin Kaepernick's
pistol read game took San Francisco to a Super Bowl, and then Buffalo's with another running quarterback, Tyrod
Taylor: the Bills led the NFL in rushing yards in 2015, and kept leading it in 2016 with the run game he had
installed, although he was fired two games into that season.[^romanbio] He was, in
other words, the league's most experienced designer of run games with a quarterback in them.

His first public description of the plan was blunt. The staff would not try to fit Jackson into something that
"other people had once done"; it would "rebuild the thing from the ground up" and build an offense "that really
accommodates" him.[^transcript] What came out of that rebuild had four pieces, and each one answers a specific
question the Chargers had asked.

**1. Heavy personnel: more blockers, and slower defenders.** The Chargers' answer had been speed: little
defenders who could run with Jackson. Roman's first move was to make little defenders expensive with
[heavy personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-heavy-personnel). The 2019
Ravens put fewer than three wide receivers on the field on `{python} pct(HEAVY.loc[2019, True])` of their
snaps, against `{python} pct(LG_HEAVY.loc[2019])` for the league, using tight ends Mark Andrews, Hayden Hurst
and Nick Boyle and the fullback (and part-time defensive lineman) Patrick Ricard
([02-01](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) has the personnel fingerprint).
Every tight end or fullback is one more blocker on a run, which forces the defense to answer with bigger
bodies. Against Baltimore in 2019, defenses were in a
[**base defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-base-defense) (four defensive backs, seven bigger front
players) on `{python} pct(BASE_BAL19)` of snaps; against the rest of the league they were in base on
`{python} pct(BASE_LG19)`.[^pers] A linebacker is a better run defender than a safety, but he is a worse
chaser of a sprinter-fast quarterback in space, and a much worse cover man against a tight end like Andrews.

**2. The pistol: no tell, and both ends in play.** The [**pistol**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pistol)
([02-02](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)) puts the quarterback about
four yards from the ball with the back directly behind him. The Ravens made it their home. In 2019 they lined up
in it on `{python} pct(PISTOL_BAL.loc[2019])` of their plays, `{python} f"{P19.iloc[0]:,}"` snaps; the rest of the
league combined used it on `{python} pct(PISTOL_LG.loc[2019])` of plays, and the next-heaviest user had
`{python} str(P19.iloc[1])` snaps all season.[^pistol] `{python} pct(PIST19_RUN)` of Baltimore's designed runs
started there. Why the pistol rather than the shotgun? Three reasons, each one a fix for something the shotgun
gives away:

- *No directional tell.* In the shotgun the back stands beside the quarterback, and which side he is on usually
  hints at where the run is going. From the pistol the back can go either way with the same first step, so the
  defense can't lean before the snap.
- *A downhill back.* A back seven yards deep and straight behind the ball runs at the line with momentum, like
  a back in the I-formation, instead of starting sideways from the quarterback's hip. That makes gap runs
  (power, counter, duo) work from the same look as reads.
- *Both ends are read keys.* With the quarterback at four yards and the back behind him, the mesh can go to
  either side, so either defensive end can be the read key on any snap. A defense that wants to tell its
  backside end to "always crash" has to tell *both* ends, and an end can't know before the snap which one he is.

**3. A menu of reads.** On top of the pistol, Roman ran the whole option family that
[03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) teaches, and added a few of his own: the zone read and
[bash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bash), the inverted veer (power read), the *counter read* (two linemen
pull and the backside end is read), *counter bash* (the back goes away from the pullers, the quarterback follows
them), and the occasional speed option.[^balreads] The point of having so many is not variety for its own
sake. Each one leaves an end alone but sends the runners to different places, so a defense that solves one
read with a stunt or an exchange ([03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#the-defense-strikes-back-the-scrape-exchange))
is wrong against the next.

**4. Designed quarterback runs: the back becomes a blocker.** And sometimes there was no read at all. Jackson
carried on purpose, on QB power, QB counter, QB draws and sweeps, and on those plays the running back or the
fullback became one more lead blocker. In 2019 Jackson had `{python} str(LJ_N.loc[2019])` designed runs, about
`{python} f"{LJ_PG.loc[2019]:.1f}"` a game, averaging `{python} f"{LJ_YPC.loc[2019]:.1f}"` yards and
`{python} sg(LJ_EPA.loc[2019])` EPA per carry.[^lj]

None of the four pieces works without the people who block for it, and the 2019 Ravens had them. Left tackle
Ronnie Stanley and right guard Marshal Yanda (his eighth Pro Bowl) were Pro Bowl starters that season, right tackle
Orlando Brown Jr. was an alternate, and Patrick Ricard went to the Pro Bowl as a fullback for his lead
blocking.[^probowl] A scheme that asks the line to block everybody but one defender needs linemen who win those
blocks.

Put those together and you have what this book calls a
[**pistol option offense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pistol-option-offense): **an offense that makes the
pistol its base alignment and builds its run game on the quarterback as a runner, with option reads and designed
quarterback runs behind extra tight ends and fullbacks, so that the defense must account for one more ball
carrier on every snap.** Chris Ault built the college version at Nevada, where the pistol was born in 2005 and
Kaepernick learned to run it ([03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#where-option-came-from-briefly)
and [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) tell that story). The 2019–2022
Ravens are the NFL's defining example.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
A pistol option offense exists because **a quarterback who is a real running threat is worth one blocker on every
run, and the pistol lets an offense collect that blocker from either side, behind a downhill back, without
showing which way it is going.** The heavy personnel makes the defense match with bigger, slower players, and
then the passing game punishes the bigger, slower players. The trade is the quarterback's body (he is a ball
carrier, or a target, on most snaps), a passing game built from fewer receivers, and a style that works best
when the offense is ahead or level, because the run is its engine.
:::

The rebuild worked at once. The 2019 Ravens went `{python} rec(2019)`, led the league in scoring with 531
points, set the NFL record for team rushing yards with 3,296, and Jackson ran for 1,206 of them, a quarterback
record, while also leading the league with 36 touchdown passes on his way to a unanimous MVP award.[^record] By
the measure this chapter uses, Baltimore's designed runs averaged `{python} sg(BAL_RUN.loc[2019, "epa"])` EPA
per play that season, `{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2019, "rank"])` in the league, while the league as a whole
averaged `{python} sg(LG_RUN.loc[2019])`. And the passing game the run was meant to open up did open up: on
dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles) the 2019 Ravens averaged `{python} sg(DB_BAL.loc[2019])` EPA per play, also
`{python} ordinal(DB_RANK.loc[2019])` in the league, against a league average of `{python} sg(DB_LG.loc[2019])`.[^db]
The rest of this chapter explains why.

## Why the quarterback changes every run fit

[Run Fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) gave the rule in one line:
count the quarterback as a blocker when he reads. It is worth slowing that down, because the Ravens' whole era is
an argument about what the rule really costs a defense, and the cost is larger than one man.

Start with a defense's ordinary plan against a run. Every gap has exactly one owner, and the defense tries to
have one more run defender than the offense has blockers: the plus-one. Against a quarterback who hands off and
watches, the plus-one is easy to find. The offense blocks as many defenders as it has blockers; the one left over
is usually the end on the far side of the play, and he can do the most useful thing a free defender can do,
chase the play down the line from behind and tackle the back if he cuts back.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fit-two-qbs
#| fig-cap: "One front, two quarterbacks. The same pistol 12-personnel look (two tight ends) against the same eight-man box (shaded), and the same inside-zone run to the right. Left: with a quarterback who only hands off, seven blockers take seven defenders and the backside end (ringed) is the defense's free man (some staffs would instead block him and leave the backside linebacker free; either way one defender is spare); he chases flat down the line and tackles the back when he cuts back. Right: with Jackson at quarterback, that end is the read key. The green branch is what happens if he chases: Jackson keeps the ball and runs where the end was. So he has to stay home and play the quarterback, and the cutback lane he would have closed stays open. Seven blockers plus a read against eight: a hat on every hat, and the defense's only spare man is a safety 12 yards away."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 3.9))
check_legal(pistol())
for ax, lamar in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(pistol(), front62(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if lamar:
        go_to(p, "BE", (0.6, -6.9), "path", speed=1.0)                 # stays home for the quarterback
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (2.2, -1.9), "path", via=[(1.7, -4.9)])         # free: chases flat down the line
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.4, -0.6), "path", speed=1.0)                # hands off and watches
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 5.8), via=[(-0.4, 5.3)])                       # reach the play-side 9
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 3.8), via=[(-0.4, 3.6)])                      # on the 5
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 2.0)])                      # on the 3
    go_to(p, "C", (3.5, 1.6), via=[(-0.3, 0.6), (0.8, 1.0)])           # climbs to the Mike
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.4, -0.5), via=[(-0.4, -1.0)])                    # on the 1
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -3.6), via=[(-0.4, -3.0)])                    # on the backside 5
    go_to(p, "U", (3.5, -2.0), via=[(-0.2, -4.3), (1.2, -3.2)])        # climbs to the Will
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-10.0, 10.0), window=(-8.6, 8.8), title=False)
    box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 5.6, -7.6, 7.6)
    if not lamar:
        # the back's cutback is drawn above the line markers so it stays visible as it crosses them
        branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.3, 1.3), (-2.8, 2.5), (-1.5, 1.7), (1.9, -0.8)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               zorder=9.5)
        tackle_x(f, p, 2.4, -1.2)
        say(f, p, -2.6, 4.7, "cuts back", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        point_to(f, p, (3.6, -7.4), (1.9, -4.4), "free: chases\nthe cutback", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
        say(f, p, -6.6, -5.6, "Q hands off\nand watches", fontsize=6.4)
        say(f, p, 6.5, 0.0, "7 blockers v 8 in the box", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        ax.set_title("A quarterback who hands off", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        read_line(f, p, (-4.0, 0.0), (1.0, -6.3))
        branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.3, 1.3), (-2.4, 2.1), (0.4, 0.6), (4.6, -0.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        branch(f, p, [(-4.0, 0.0), (-3.7, -2.4), (-1.8, -6.0), (0.4, -7.9), (2.8, -8.3)], color=GREEN)
        say(f, p, -3.7, -6.7, "keep, if\nhe chases", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.3, weight="bold")
        point_to(f, p, (4.9, -6.4), (1.2, -6.6), "must stay\nfor the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
        say(f, p, -6.6, -5.6, "Q reads the 9", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.4)
        say(f, p, 6.5, 0.0, "7 blockers + a read v 8", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        ax.set_title("Jackson at quarterback", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Now put Jackson at quarterback (@fig-fit-two-qbs, right). Nothing about the blocking changes, but the free man
isn't free any more. If the backside end chases the back, Jackson keeps the ball and runs into the space the end
just left. So the end has to stay home and play the quarterback, and the moment he does, the defense has lost
its plus-one: seven blockers and a read against eight defenders is a hat on every hat. To get the plus-one back,
the defense has to bring a ninth defender down, and in @fig-fit-two-qbs the only one left is the free safety,
twelve yards deep and the last man in the deep middle.

That is the arithmetic. The Ravens' insight was that the arithmetic doesn't only apply on read plays. It
applies on **every** run, for three reasons that compound.

**The threat works on plays that aren't reads.** Most of the Ravens' runs were simple handoffs. But a backside
end can't see the play call. On every pistol handoff he sees the same mesh he sees on a read, and if he chases the
back on the one snap in five that was a read, Jackson is gone. So he learns to stay home *every* time, and on the
four plain handoffs the offense gets for free what it earned on the read: an end who isn't chasing the
cutback. Coaches call this "freezing" the backside, and it is why a quarterback's run threat improves his running
backs' numbers even when he never touches the ball.

**Every defender's fit gets one more line.** A run fit
([05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)) is a list of who owns which gap.
Against a running quarterback, the defense needs one more owner on that list, *quarterback*, on every play, and
the person who owns him can't own anything else. If it's the end, he can't squeeze; if it's a linebacker, his gap
needs a new owner; if it's a safety, the deep middle does. There is no free version.

**Pursuit stops being free.** Even after the ball is handed off, a defense normally gets a bonus: everybody on the
far side of the play turns and runs to the ball. That backside pursuit cleans up mistakes. Against Jackson,
backside defenders who turn and run before they're sure the quarterback doesn't have it get punished by the keep,
so they turn a step later, and a step later is the difference between a four-yard run and a twelve-yard one.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Loading the box stops a running quarterback." Loading the box is how a defense gets its plus-one against a
handoff. Against a quarterback who reads, an eight-man box is a seven-man box, because one of the eight is
assigned to the quarterback. In fact, the 2019 Ravens saw loaded boxes about as often as everyone else did
(eight or more defenders on `{python} pct(BOX8_BAL.loc[2019])` of their designed runs, against
`{python} pct(BOX8_LG.loc[2019])` for the league), and still led the league in rushing efficiency. What defenses did
differently against Baltimore was get *bigger*, not more numerous: base personnel on
`{python} pct(BASE_BY.loc[2019, True])` of snaps against `{python} pct(BASE_BY.loc[2019, False])` against everyone
else, a gap that held through Roman's four seasons. The boxes got heavier later: in 2021 and 2022 Baltimore saw eight
or more on `{python} pct(BOX8_BAL.loc[2021])` and `{python} pct(BOX8_BAL.loc[2022])` of its designed runs, against
about `{python} pct(BOX8_LG.loc[2021:2022].mean())` for the league, and its runs still ranked
`{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2021, "rank"])` and `{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2022, "rank"])`.[^box] The extra
defender has to come from somewhere, and when he comes from the deep secondary, the passing game is aimed at the
hole he leaves.
:::

## Signature play 1: the pistol inverted veer

The play that best shows Roman's design is the inverted veer, the
[power read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-power-read), run from the pistol with two tight ends.
[03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#inverted-veer-the-quarterback-goes-inside) drew it from
the shotgun with a slot receiver; the Ravens' version shows what the pistol and the extra tight ends add.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pistol-iv
#| fig-cap: "The pistol inverted veer (power read) to the right, from 12 personnel against an eight-man box. The line blocks power: the right tight end (Y) blocks down on the 5, the right tackle and right guard double-team the 3 before the guard climbs to the Will, the center blocks back on the 1, and the left guard pulls across for the Mike. On the backside, the left tackle and the other tight end (U) wall off the 5 and the 9. The play-side 9 (ringed), the end man on the line outside the tight end, is the one defender not blocked: Jackson reads him. The back, starting directly behind the quarterback, comes around his right hip for the mesh and sweeps wide. If the 9 widens with the back, Jackson keeps and runs inside him, a step behind the pulling guard (green); if the 9 squeezes inside, Jackson gives and the back runs outside him (dark), where the play-side wide receiver (out of the picture) blocks the cornerback. Count the box: seven blockers and a read against eight. The free safety, the only defender left, is 12 yards deep (out of the picture)."
p = Play(pistol(), front62(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 4.1), via=[(-0.3, 4.5)])                               # down on the 5
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.7), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])                              # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.4, 2.0), (1.4, 0.8)])     # double the 3, climb to the Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))                                                 # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.8), via=[(-0.6, -3.5)])                            # hinge on the backside 5
go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -6.0), via=[(-0.4, -5.3)])                             # wall off the backside 9
go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, 3.3), "pull", via=[(-2.2, -1.3), (-2.7, 0.9), (-1.9, 3.4), (-0.3, 5.0), (1.6, 4.6)])
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-9.0, 14.5), window=(-8.6, 9.0), title=False, width_in=5.8)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 5.8, -7.6, 7.6)
read_line(f, p, (-4.0, 0.3), (0.6, 6.0))
branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.0, 0.6), (-4.4, 1.4), (-3.7, 4.2), (-2.7, 8.4), (-0.6, 10.7), (5.4, 11.5)],
       color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="give if the 9\nsqueezes", label_at=(-5.9, 10.4), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-4.0, 0.0), (-3.7, 1.6), (-3.0, 3.5), (-1.5, 4.9), (0.3, 5.7), (6.0, 5.7)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the 9\nwidens", label_at=(7.0, 2.6), fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-2.6, -6.6), (-2.3, -1.0), "LG pulls\nfor the Mike", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -4.4), (-6.9, -0.5), "R: behind Q,\nno tell", fontsize=6.4)
say(f, p, 7.2, -4.6, "8 in the box v\n7 blockers + a read", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
f.ax.set_title("Pistol inverted veer (power read), 12 personnel", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK,
               fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

Walk through what @fig-pistol-iv asks of the defense.

**Before the snap, the defense can't lean.** In the shotgun, a back offset to the left usually means a run to
the right; from the pistol, the back is straight behind the quarterback and gives nothing away. The defense has
to stay balanced: a 9 on each side, a 5 on each side, linebackers over the middle.

**At the snap, the line tells a story of power.** The tight end and tackle block down, a guard pulls across.
A linebacker who reads the guards has been taught to follow a pulling guard, because on power the puller leads the
ball carrier through the hole. Here he does lead a ball carrier through the hole, but which one?

**The end man has a bad choice.** The play-side 9 is the man the power play would normally kick out, or
[log](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-log-block) (seal inside from the outside so the runner can bounce around
him). On this play nobody touches him. If he does what he's taught against power, *squeeze* the hole from the
outside so the pulling guard has nowhere to go, he has stepped inside the back, who is running outside him at full
speed. Out there the play-side wide receiver blocks the cornerback, and the back's problem is the
[alley player](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alley-player), usually a safety coming down from depth. If he widens to take the back, he has opened the hole for the
quarterback, who follows the guard through it. Either way the defense's best edge player is blocked by
a decision.

Why build it from the pistol with tight ends instead of the shotgun with receivers, as most college teams did? The
tight ends do two jobs a receiver can't. The play-side tight end's down block on the 5 creates the hole's inside
wall from a tighter angle, so the quarterback's keep lane is a real gap, not a crease. And the backside tight end
blocks a man a receiver couldn't: the backside 9, the defender who on a shotgun power read is left to chase the
quarterback from behind. With him walled off, **the eight-man box is fully accounted for**, seven blocks and a
read, which is the arithmetic of @fig-fit-two-qbs made into a play.

What does it cost? Two things. The back is running sideways on the give, so a wrong read (a give when the 9 was
actually widening) loses yards. And the keep sends Jackson between the tackles, where the linebackers and the
safety arrive, on every snap that the 9 widens. That second cost is real enough that the Ravens ran the play
in measured doses, which brings us to the formation that made the doses unpredictable.

## Signature play 2: the 13-personnel sets

The most extreme version of Roman's heavy offense put three tight ends on the field:
[**13 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-13-personnel), one back, three tight ends and one wide
receiver. In 2019 it was a small slice of the Ravens' offense, a few dozen regular-season snaps, but
it is the clearest picture of the bind the whole offense put defenses in, and it hides a surprise.

```{python}
#| label: fig-13-plate
#| fig-cap: "The 13-personnel bind, as the 2019 Ravens used it (illustrative; in 2019 the three tight ends were typically Mark Andrews, Nick Boyle and Hayden Hurst, with Mark Ingram at running back and the lone wide receiver off the line as a flanker, out of the picture). Both panels show the same pistol formation, with the U and Y tight ends on the line and H on the wing, against the defense's usual answer: a base 4-3, eight in the box (shaded) and one deep safety. The Sam already sits over the wing on the strong side, so the strong safety walks down on the other side, outside U, to give each side the same number of defenders. Left, the pass: after a run fake (the ball's flight is the dotted brown line from the quarterback), the Y runs up the seam against a linebacker in man coverage (dotted orange). The only man behind him is the free safety, who has to hold the middle against the fake and arrives late. Right, the run: seven linemen and tight ends plus the wing make eight blockers for eight defenders before the quarterback reads anyone. Jackson reads the backside 5 (ringed) and the U arcs past him to the safety, so the defense is a man short until the free safety comes down, and the free safety is the man the pass in the left panel is aimed at."
def plate():
    off = pistol(extra=(O("H", "TE", -1.6, 6.6, "H"),))
    check_legal(off)
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "5"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT3", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "9"), D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 8.2, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -6.8, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.8, 0.0, "FS")]
    return Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 4.7))
# left: play-action seam
p = plate()
go_to(p, "RB", (-5.2, -2.6), "path", via=[(-5.6, -0.8)])          # run fake to the left
p.route("Y", [(5.0, 0.4), (13.0, 0.9)])
p.man("MIKE", "Y")
go_to(p, "FS", (12.6, 3.8), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.5)
for k, end in [("LT", (-0.6, -3.4)), ("LG", (-0.6, -1.5)), ("C", (-0.7, 0.0)), ("RG", (-0.6, 1.6)),
               ("RT", (-0.7, 3.3)), ("U", (-0.8, -4.9)), ("H", (-0.9, 6.0))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, 2.2), "path", speed=3.0, via=[(-4.5, -0.9)])
p.pass_to("Y", t=2.2)
p.highlight("Y", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-10.0, 11.0), window=(-8.6, 15.6), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 6.2, -8.4, 9.4)
point_to(f, p, (8.0, -5.6), (7.0, 5.4), "Y on a\nlinebacker", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, -6.4, -6.4, "run fake", fontsize=6.4)
say(f, p, 13.2, -6.0, "one safety deep", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axes[0].set_title("The pass: the seam", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
# right: the run, eight blockers and a read
p = plate()
go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 6.1), via=[(-0.3, 5.4)])                      # reach the 9
go_to(p, "H", (3.6, 7.9), via=[(0.2, 7.2)])                       # lead up on the Sam
go_to(p, "RT", (3.4, 2.4), via=[(-0.3, 3.4), (0.8, 3.0)])         # combo, climbs to the Mike
go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 2.0)])                     # on the 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.4), via=[(-0.3, 0.2)])                     # on the 1
go_to(p, "LG", (0.3, -0.9), via=[(-0.3, -1.3)])                   # helps on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (3.6, -2.0), via=[(-0.3, -2.6), (0.8, -2.6)])      # climbs to the Will
go_to(p, "U", (4.8, -6.6), via=[(-0.2, -5.6), (1.6, -7.0)])       # arcs past the read end to the safety
p.highlight("LE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-10.0, 11.0), window=(-8.6, 15.6), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 6.2, -8.4, 9.4)
read_line(f, p, (-4.0, 0.0), (1.0, -4.0))
branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.3, 1.3), (-1.6, 2.1), (4.6, 1.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
branch(f, p, [(-4.0, 0.0), (-3.6, -2.6), (-1.6, -5.0), (0.6, -5.4), (4.4, -4.6)], color=GREEN)
say(f, p, 9.2, 1.0, "8 blockers + a read\nv 8 in the box", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.7, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-6.4, -6.2), (-0.5, -5.6), "U arcs\nto the SS", fontsize=6.4)
axes[1].set_title("The run: one man short", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-13-plate as the defense's coordinator, on the sideline, deciding what to put on the field when three
tight ends run on.

**If he plays it as a run formation**, with base personnel and eight in the box (defenses chose base on about
`{python} pct(P13_BASE)` of Baltimore's `{python} str(len(P13))` such snaps in 2019, a small sample, so read every
13-personnel number here as a tendency), he is still a man short against the run (right panel):
eight blockers plus Jackson's read against eight. To get even he needs the free safety in the box, and then
nobody is deep. Meanwhile his linebackers are covering tight ends. Mark Andrews, who led the 2019 Ravens in
catches, was a 6-foot-5 receiver in a tight end's job description; a linebacker in man coverage on him up the
seam (left panel) is the mismatch the formation was built to create.

**If he plays it as a pass formation**, with smaller players to cover the tight ends, the run arithmetic gets
worse: smaller defenders to block, and seven of them in the box against eight blockers and a read.

And here is the surprise. The league ran the ball on about `{python} pct(1 - L13_PASS)` of its 13-personnel
snaps in 2019, as you'd expect from a goal-line-looking grouping. **Baltimore threw on
`{python} pct(P13_PASS)` of them.**[^p13] Three tight ends didn't mean "run" for the Ravens any more than three
wide receivers meant "pass": that season they ran on `{python} pct(P11_RUN_BAL)` of their 11-personnel snaps
(three receivers), against `{python} pct(P11_RUN_LG)` for the league. The personnel stopped being a tell. That is
the deepest point of Roman's design: once the quarterback is a runner, every grouping can run, so every grouping
can also throw, and a defense that reads personnel to guess run or pass, as
[02-01](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) teaches you to, guesses wrong more often
against Baltimore than against anyone.

## Signature play 3: the QB counter

The third signature play has no read at all. On the **QB counter**, Jackson is the ball carrier from the snap,
the running back is a decoy and then a blocker, and two blockers pull across the formation to lead him.
[03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#designed-quarterback-runs-adding-a-blocker) drew a
shotgun version with a guard and tackle pulling. The Ravens' favourite version used what they had most of: a
tight end as the second puller.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-counter
#| fig-cap: "QB counter from the pistol, 12 personnel, to the right (simulated, in Big Data Bowl coordinates; purple rings mark the two pullers, the green ring the ball, faint lines where each player has been). 1, the snap: eight defenders in the box, the back directly behind the quarterback. 2, Jackson and the back take a step to the left, selling a run that way; the two linebackers take a false step with them (the Mike's faint trail points left), while the left guard and the backside tight end (U) start pulling right behind the line. 3, the guard kicks out the play-side 9 outside the Y's down block; the tight end turns up through the hole the down blocks have made, leading for the quarterback. 4, Jackson follows a step behind the tight end into the second level, where the Mike, who first stepped the wrong way, has to take on a blocker; the right guard has climbed to the Will, and the back has turned around to block the backside 9. Eight blockers for eight defenders, with the quarterback carrying: the running back's block is the hat a handoff can't provide."
def qb_counter():
    p = Play(pistol(), front62(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # the defense: linebackers take a real false step with the fake, then react; the play-side 9 squeezes
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.2, 6.9), "path", speed=1.0, delay=0.2)        # fights outside the kick-out
    go_to(p, "P5", (1.4, 3.3), "path", speed=0.7, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "DT3", (1.4, 2.0), "path", speed=0.7, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "DT1", (1.2, -0.3), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "B5", (1.0, -4.0), "path", speed=0.6)
    go_to(p, "BE", (-0.6, -6.0), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (4.0, -3.8), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)                  # false step with the back
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.2, 0.0), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)                   # false step...
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.6, 2.8), "path", speed=2.2, delay=0.25)                  # ...then back to the play
    # the offense (GY counter: down blocks on the play side, C back, the uncovered RG to the backside LB)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 3.9), via=[(-0.3, 4.4)], speed=1.6)                       # down on the 5
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.2, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 2.9)], speed=1.6)                      # down on the 3
    go_to(p, "C", (0.1, -0.9), speed=1.4)                                         # back on the 1
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.0, -2.9), via=[(-0.2, 1.0), (1.0, 0.0)], speed=2.6)        # climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.1, -3.4), speed=1.0)                                       # on the backside 5
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.0, 6.4), "pull", via=[(-1.8, -1.1), (-2.1, 2.4), (-0.8, 5.2)], speed=5.2)   # kick out the 9
    go_to(p, "U", (3.4, 3.2), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -4.0), (-2.4, 1.0), (-1.2, 4.8), (0.8, 5.0)], speed=6.4)  # lead up
    go_to(p, "RB", (-6.4, -1.9), "path", speed=3.0)                              # the counter step
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, -5.2), speed=4.6)                                      # then block the backside 9
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.4, -1.3), "path", speed=2.4)                              # step left with the back
    go_to(p, "QB", (5.8, 4.9), "run", speed=5.6, delay=0.35,
          via=[(-3.8, 0.8), (-2.2, 3.0), (-0.8, 4.8), (1.0, 5.1)])
    return p


play_animation(qb_counter(), [0.0, 0.6, 1.9, 2.7], lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-8.2, 7.8),
               notes=["Eight in the box; the back\nis right behind the QB",
                      "QB and back step left;\nthe LBs step with them",
                      "The guard kicks out the 9; the\ntight end leads up the hole",
                      "QB follows the tight end;\nthe back blocks the backside 9"],
               rings=(("LG", PURPLE), ("U", PURPLE)), ncols=2)
```

Three things make this play the Ravens' and not just anyone's.

**The fake beats both kinds of linebacker.** Linebackers are taught to read one of two things at the snap
(their [key](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)), and the counter
beats each one differently. A linebacker who keys the *backfield* reads the running back: if he steps left, the run
is going left. Against Jackson he also has to wonder whether the quarterback is about to keep the ball and run left
himself, so his false step left is bigger, and the cutback right, which is where the counter goes, is bigger too.
A linebacker who keys the *guards* is not fooled about the direction: he sees the guard and the tight end pull right,
and the pullers tell the truth. What beats him is the half-second of doubt before he trusts them. The mesh looks like
every read play he has seen, and if he flies after the pullers and Jackson hands the ball off going left, he has
run himself out of the play. So he hesitates for a beat, and a beat is all the tight end needs to arrive at him with
a head of steam.

**The pullers are a tight end and a guard, not two linemen.** Many counter plays pull the backside guard and
tackle. Pulling the tackle leaves a second hole in the backside of the line, where he used to stand, that someone
has to step back and fill so a defender can't run through it into the backfield. Pulling the backside
*tight end* instead keeps the tackle home on the 5, and the tight end is usually the better athlete for the second
puller's job: turning up through the hole and finding a linebacker in space. The running back, after his fake,
turns around and blocks the backside 9 (@fig-qb-counter, panel 4), the job he would have on any counter. Count the
blocks: eight, against eight. That is the designed-run arithmetic of
[03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#designed-quarterback-runs-adding-a-blocker) with the
Ravens' extra tight end supplying the eighth.

**It punishes the defense for following the rules.** The linebackers who follow the first flow are doing what
they're coached to do. The 9 who squeezes the down blocks is doing what he's coached to do. Both are wrong,
because the play is built to make their rules point the wrong way. That is the pattern of the whole offense: not
a trick, but a set of plays where each defender's textbook reaction is the one the next play attacks.

The price is the one the "Why it exists" box named: Jackson is a ball carrier between the tackles, so the Ravens
rationed these runs. How much they rationed them, and how that changed, is in the data.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco at Baltimore, December 1, 2019 (watching the pistol)"}
Earlier chapters showed these Ravens' personnel, early downs, reads and boxes; this time, watch the pistol itself,
in the game that shows it best. The 10–1 49ers, the eventual NFC champions, came to Baltimore on a rainy
40-degree afternoon. The Ravens lined up in the pistol on `{python} pct(SF19["pistol"])` of their snaps, their
highest share of the season, and called a designed run on `{python} pct(SF19["run_rate"])` of their plays; Jackson
ran 16 times for 101 yards, every carry a designed run. With 4:39 left and the score tied, he converted a
fourth-and-1 at his own 44 on a run behind the right guard, and Justin Tucker won it 20–17 with a 49-yard field goal
as time expired.[^sf19]

**What to notice:** before each snap, note where the back is. Behind Jackson (pistol) is the base look, and in this
game it was seven snaps in ten. Then, at the snap, watch the **two ends** rather than the
ball. One of them is being read and the other is being blocked, and you can usually tell which within a step:
the read end is the one nobody touches. Over a quarter, notice how rarely either end chases the back flat down the
line. That restraint, the frozen backside, is the hidden yardage of the whole offense: it is there on the plain
handoffs too.
:::

## The data fingerprint

How good was the Ravens' run game, how long did it last, and how did it change? Play-by-play data can't see a
read, but it can see the results. @fig-rush-epa compares Baltimore's designed runs with every other team's,
season by season, using EPA per play.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-epa
#| fig-cap: "Rushing efficiency, regular seasons 2018–2025: EPA per designed run (quarterback scrambles, kneel-downs and botched snaps excluded) for every team (gray dots), the league average (gray line) and Baltimore (blue, with its league rank). In 2018 Jackson started only the last seven games; 2021 and 2022 were cut short by his injuries in December. Shaded bands mark the two offensive coordinators of the era. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy."
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.axvspan(2018.5, 2022.5, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.06, lw=0)
ax.axvspan(2022.5, 2025.5, color=style.SERIES[1], alpha=0.06, lw=0)
for s in SEASONS:
    v = TEAM_RUN[(TEAM_RUN["season"] == s) & (TEAM_RUN["posteam"] != "BAL")]["epa"]
    ax.scatter(np.full(len(v), s) + np.random.default_rng(s).uniform(-0.14, 0.14, len(v)), v, s=9,
               color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=2)
ax.plot(LG_RUN.index, LG_RUN.values, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
ax.plot(BAL_RUN.index, BAL_RUN["epa"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=5, zorder=4)
for s, r in BAL_RUN.iterrows():
    off2021 = s == 2021                                   # 2021 sits among the gray dots: label it to the right
    ax.annotate(ordinal(r["rank"]), (s, r["epa"]), xytext=(7, 0) if off2021 else (0, 7), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="left" if off2021 else "center", va="center" if off2021 else "bottom",
                fontsize=7.5, color=style.SERIES[0], fontweight="bold",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85) if off2021 else None)
ax.annotate("Baltimore", (2025, BAL_RUN.loc[2025, "epa"]), xytext=(10, -2), textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=8, color=style.SERIES[0], va="center")
ax.annotate("league average", (2025, LG_RUN.loc[2025]), xytext=(10, -2), textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.text(2020.5, 0.235, "Roman OC, 2019–2022", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(2024.0, 0.235, "Monken OC, 2023–2025", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
ax.annotate("Henry\narrives", (2024, BAL_RUN.loc[2024, "epa"]), xytext=(2023.25, 0.17), fontsize=7,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
ax.set_xlim(2017.6, 2026.6)
ax.set_ylim(-0.27, 0.26)
ax.set_xticks(SEASONS)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per designed run", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Four things stand out in @fig-rush-epa.

**It was the best run game of its time, and it stayed that way.** Baltimore's designed runs ranked
`{python} ", ".join(ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[s, "rank"]) for s in range(2019, 2026))` in the league from 2019 to
2025, and were above the league average every season. In a league where the average designed run *loses*
expected points (the gray line sits below zero every year), the Ravens' runs gained them in every season but 2021,
under two coordinators, with five different leading running backs (Mark Ingram, J. K. Dobbins, Devonta Freeman,
Gus Edwards and Derrick Henry). Their [success rates](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate) tell the same
story. A run is "successful" when its EPA is positive, meaning it left the offense better off than before the
snap; more than `{python} pct(min(BAL_SR.loc[2019:2025]))` of
Baltimore's designed runs were successful every season, against a league that hovered around
`{python} pct(LG_SR.loc[2019:2025].mean())`.

**2018 was a different offense halfway through.** The season's dot mixes ten weeks of Flacco with seven of
Jackson; the split earlier in the chapter (from `{python} sg(R18["flacco"][1])` to
`{python} sg(R18["jackson"][1])` per run) is the real story.

**The dip is the injuries.** 2021 is the one season the Ravens' runs were merely average
(`{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2021, "rank"])`). Jackson played `{python} str(LJ_GAMES.loc[2021])` games before
an ankle injury in December ended his season, the team lost its top two running backs before the season began,
and Baltimore finished `{python} rec(2021)`.[^injuries] 2022 ended the same way, with Jackson hurt in December
and backup Tyler Huntley starting the wild-card loss in Cincinnati. Even so, the run game ranked
`{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2022, "rank"])` that year. (A footnote on the cost the chapter keeps naming, the
quarterback's body: neither season-ending injury came on a designed run. The 2021 ankle injury came on a completed
pass at Cleveland, and the 2022 knee injury on a sack against Denver. A running quarterback takes more hits, but the
pocket is not safe either.) The 2021 line was weakened too: left tackle Ronnie Stanley, back from the ankle injury
that had ended his 2020 season, played only the opener before more surgery ended his year.[^stanley]

**Two coordinators, one result, different recipes.** The top of the chart is level across the change of
coordinator in 2023, which can make it look as if nothing changed. A great deal did. @fig-fingerprint shows the
recipes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fingerprint
#| fig-cap: "How the run game was built, 2018–2025 regular seasons (Baltimore in blue, league average in gray). Top left: Jackson's designed runs (no scrambles, botched snaps or likely sneaks) per game he played. Top right: share of plays with fewer than three wide receivers. Bottom left: share of plays from the pistol (Next Gen Stats formation labels through 2022, FTN charting from 2023; the vertical line marks the change of source). The two sources disagree a little, so the hollow diamond adds FTN's own 2022 figure: measured the same way both years, Baltimore's pistol share still fell from about a quarter of its plays to under a tenth, so the drop is real and not an artifact of the new source. Bottom right: share of plays with the quarterback under center (FTN charting, 2022–2025 only). Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting via nflreadpy."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.9))
blue, gray = style.SERIES[0], style.MUTED


def two_lines(ax, xs, bal, lg, title, fmt="{:.0%}", ymax=None):
    ax.plot(xs, lg, color=gray, lw=1.6, marker="o", ms=3)
    ax.plot(xs, bal, color=blue, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    if ymax:
        ax.set_ylim(0, ymax)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: fmt.format(v)))


ax = axes[0, 0]
ax.bar(LJ_PG.index, LJ_PG.values, color=[blue if s != 2018 else "#9ec5f4" for s in LJ_PG.index], width=0.7)
for s, v in LJ_PG.items():
    ax.text(s, v + 0.15, f"{v:.1f}", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_title("Jackson's designed runs per game", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
two_lines(axes[0, 1], SEASONS, [HEAVY.loc[s, True] for s in SEASONS], LG_HEAVY.values,
          "Plays with fewer than 3 WRs", ymax=0.95)
ax = axes[1, 0]
pist_bal = [PISTOL_BAL.get(s, np.nan) if s <= 2022 else QBLOC.loc[(s, True), "P"] for s in SEASONS]
pist_lg = [PISTOL_LG.get(s, np.nan) if s <= 2022 else
           (QBLOC.loc[(s, False), "P"]) for s in SEASONS]
two_lines(ax, SEASONS, pist_bal, pist_lg, "Plays from the pistol", ymax=0.62)
ax.axvline(2022.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(2022.6, 0.56, "NGS | FTN", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED)
# FTN also charted 2022: plot it as a hollow marker so the 2022 -> 2023 drop can be read like for like
ax.plot([2022, 2023], [QBLOC.loc[(2022, True), "P"], QBLOC.loc[(2023, True), "P"]], color=blue, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)))
ax.plot([2022], [QBLOC.loc[(2022, True), "P"]], marker="D", ms=4.5, mfc="white", mec=blue, mew=1.3, ls="none")
ax.annotate("2022 by FTN", (2022, QBLOC.loc[(2022, True), "P"]), xytext=(2019.2, 0.15), fontsize=6.3,
            color=blue, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=blue, lw=0.6))
ax = axes[1, 1]
yrs = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
two_lines(ax, yrs, [QBLOC.loc[(s, True), "U"] for s in yrs], [QBLOC.loc[(s, False), "U"] for s in yrs],
          "Plays under center", ymax=0.45)
ax.set_xticks(yrs)
ax.set_xlim(2021.6, 2025.4)
for a in (axes[0, 0], axes[0, 1], axes[1, 0]):
    a.set_xticks([2018, 2020, 2022, 2024])
axes[0, 1].text(2018.1, 0.86, "Baltimore", color=blue, fontsize=7.5, fontweight="bold")
axes[0, 1].text(2018.1, 0.12, "league", color=gray, fontsize=7.5, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

Read the four panels of @fig-fingerprint as three eras.

**The Roman years (2019–2022): the pistol option offense at full strength.** Jackson averaged between
`{python} f"{LJ_PG.loc[2019:2022].min():.1f}"` and `{python} f"{LJ_PG.loc[2019:2022].max():.1f}"` designed runs a
game. The pistol was the base alignment (bottom left), at many times the league's rate. And heavy personnel
